stem.text: Five years ago the Gini coefficient of a county was 0.35 but now it is 0.40.
Which combination of policies is most likely to have been used in the last five years?

explanation.text: A Gini coefficient rising from 0.35 to 0.40 means income inequality has increased. Each of the three policy changes needs to independently push toward greater inequality: lower corporate taxes tend to benefit firm owners and shareholders (higher-income groups) relatively more; higher sales taxes are regressive, taking a larger share of income from lower earners who spend a greater proportion of their income; and a real-terms cut to means-tested benefits directly reduces the income of the poorest households who rely on them.

optionAnalysis.text: Decreasing sales taxes (less regressive burden on lower earners) and increasing benefits in real terms (more support for the poor) both work to reduce inequality, contradicting the rising Gini coefficient; only the corporate tax cut points the other way.

All three changes point toward greater inequality: lower corporate taxes favour higher-income owners, higher (regressive) sales taxes burden lower earners proportionally more, and a real cut in means-tested benefits reduces the income of the poorest.

Decreasing sales taxes and decreasing benefits pull in opposite directions (one reduces, one increases inequality), and the corporate tax rise (likely falling more on owners) would reduce inequality too, so this combination does not consistently explain a rising Gini coefficient.
Increasing means-tested benefits in real terms reduces inequality, directly contradicting a rising Gini coefficient, even though the other two changes point toward greater inequality.

reasoningChain: Recall that a higher Gini coefficient means more income inequality.
Assess each policy instrument's typical distributional effect: corporate tax cuts favour the better-off; higher sales tax is regressive; benefit cuts hurt the poorest.
Select the only option where all three changes consistently push toward greater inequality, matching the observed rise in the Gini coefficient.

inferredMistakes.text: Treating a cut to corporate tax as pro-poor (e.g. assuming it boosts jobs/wages) rather than recognising its typical distributional effect favours capital owners, a higher-income group, over workers.
